note: Prototype one household Nestor memory shared by Cursor, Claude, and a loopback local model. The model is brought closer to the work without moving the authority boundary: deterministic hooks decide what may run, Nestor serves signed guidance, Ollama drafts within bounded caller-supplied context, and a human remains the only source of a seal.

decisions.question: How do Cursor, Claude, and local models stay on the same page without sharing authority?
decisions.commitment: They open one explicitly pinned household database and ledger under ~/.nestor, verify the same public Ed25519 keys, and load one repository-owned semantic hook manifest compiled into each client's dialect. Private signing material remains in the human browser; generated client configuration is transport, not policy.
decisions.why: Separate client stores would turn agreement into an import/synchronization problem and permit each agent to accumulate a different history. Sharing the signed read/propose surface gives every client the same verified capital while signatures and the absent sealing tool preserve the difference between common context and common authority.

decisions.question: Where may a local model participate in the agent loop?
decisions.commitment: A loopback-only nestor_draft tool may retrieve signed guidance and return a bounded analysis or patch suggestion with model and prompt provenance. It receives no filesystem, shell, nested-tool, non-loopback network, verification, or automatic queue authority. Queueing remains the separate explicit nestor_propose action.
decisions.why: The useful experiment is whether verified context lets a small local model handle routine work. Letting model output decide permissions, execute its suggestion, or label itself verified would test a different proposition by removing the boundary Nestor exists to preserve. Separate drafting from application and proposal so each transition remains visible and testable.

decisions.question: Who owns cross-client hook wiring?
decisions.commitment: The repository owns semantic policy and refusals; willow-mcp owns compilation into Cursor and Claude JSON, identity/path substitution, atomic writes, and drift reporting. Unsupported client events are reported rather than silently omitted.
decisions.why: A fleet template previously overwrote Nestor's local Cursor wiring with generic Willow hooks. Putting policy in the generator would let infrastructure weaken a repository boundary; putting dialect details in every repository recreates drift. A checked-in neutral manifest makes the ownership line executable.

decisions.question: How is the first public-only browser verifier keyring bootstrapped?
decisions.commitment: The human initializes a valid empty keyring with the non-clobbering `nestor keys init`, starts the UI with that keyring configured, generates a non-extractable browser identity, enrolls only the printed public half out of band, and restarts the UI so its deliberately cached trust root includes the new verifier.
decisions.why: Starting with a missing configured keyring correctly refuses, while starting with no keyring hides identity controls; manual shell redirection can solve that circularity once but destroys enrolled keys when repeated. A first-class idempotent initializer makes the one-time bootstrap explicit without minting signing authority or weakening the missing-keyring refusal.
